speaker: Kimberly
en: Welcome to REWORK, a podcast by 37signals about the better way to work and run your business. I’m Kimberly Rhodes back again with our co-founders of 37signals, Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson. This week I thought we’d talk a little bit about the idea of one-way doors versus two-way doors. We’ve talked about that before from Jeff Bezos’ famous quotes. But it’s funny because I’ve been thinking, over the last 25 years that this business has been a business, you guys often say no decisions are that big of a deal. We can change our mind at any time. I thought we would talk about that because I don’t think most companies feel like all these decisions are irreversible. Are there any decisions you guys can think about in the last 25 years that were big decisions, hard decisions that you couldn’t come back from?
zh: 欢迎来到 REWORK，这是由 37signals 制作的关于更好工作和经营方式的播客。我是 Kimberly Rhodes，再次回到我们的 37signals �

speaker: Jason
en: Well, we’ve made a few. Selling a piece of the company to Jeff Bezos in 2006 was one, and that just changed the cap table a little bit.
zh: 我们做过几个。2006 年把公司的一部分卖给 Jeff Bezos 是其中之一，这只是稍微改变了股权结构表。

speaker: Kimberly
en: Okay, let’s talk about that really quick.
zh: 好吧，让我们快速谈谈这件事。

speaker: Jason
en: Yeah
zh: 是的。

speaker: Kimberly
en: When that happened, was that a, we need to think about this for a long time and discuss it and write the pros and cons? Or was it like a quick decision for the two of you?
zh: 当那发生时，那是我们需要花很长时间思考、讨论并列出利弊清单的事吗？还是对你们两个人来说是个快速的决定？

speaker: Jason
en: I don’t recall exactly how many conversations we had about it, but we’d had not a hundred, but we had many, many, many, many people ask us if they could buy in and we said no. And then Jeff felt different. We met him a couple times. We went out to Seattle to meet him. It just kind of felt right and we just had to find a way to do it. I don’t remember if we sat around debating it that much still. I don’t remember. Do you remember, David? I felt like it was just kinda, ultimately just sort of made sense and we figured out could we do this or not?
zh: 我不记得我们到底有过多少次对话，但不是一百次，而是有非常、非常多、非常多的人问我们是否可以买入，我们都说不行。然后 Jeff 感觉不同。我们见过他几次。我们去了西雅图见他。感觉就是对的，我们只是必须找到办法去做。我不记得我们是否围着它争论了那么久。我不记得了。你记得吗，David？我感觉这最终只是有点道理，我们搞清楚能不能这么做？

speaker: David
en: I don’t recall any pro and con lists, but I also don’t recall any pro and con list about anything we’ve ever decided to do.
zh: 我不记得有任何利弊清单，但我也不记得对于我们决定做的任何事有任何利弊清单。

speaker: Jason
en: Yeah, we don’t work that way.
zh: 是的，我们不那样工作。

speaker: David
en: We don’t work that way and we don’t think that way. But I do think in terms of the decisions, if you tally them all up, this one would be in the top five, maybe top three of most consequential decisions that we at least at the time contemplated a fair bit. Now we’ve contemplated other things even more since that seemed even less consequential. But at the time it was clear that if you let someone buy a slice of your company, well ta-da, they’re now your co-owner. And co-ownership comes with a lot of obligations and responsibilities to those owners. And in theory, at least a bunch of restrictions on what you can and cannot do. And I think that more than anything was what held us back for a hot moment and why we said no to so many others, that we were not willing to sell that independence and ability to do whatever the hell we wanted, whenever the hell we wanted.
zh: 我们不那样工作，我们也不那样思考。但我确实认为在决定方面，如果你把它们全部加起来，这一决定将排在前五名，也许前三名，是当时我们至少考虑了相当多的最重要的决定之一。现在我们考虑过其他更多的事情，因为那些看起来更不重要。但在当时很清楚，如果你让别人买下你公司的一块，瞧，他们现在是你公司的共同所有者。共同所有权伴随着对这些所有者的大量义务和责任。理论上，至少有一堆关于你能做什么和不能做什么的限制。我认为最重要的是让我们犹豫了片刻的原因，也是我们对其他许多其他人说不的原因，

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think this was also why the Bezos deal eventually ended up closing was that Jeff was not actually interested in buying our independence. He was not interested in buying into a set of rights of telling us what to do, which would characterize, I think, most of the VCs we talked to at the time otherwise. But it was also just a fact of, hey, this is a big check. And neither Jason or I, and even less so me at the time had much money to our names. And I think we had the humility to think, do you know what? This could very well end. Most things end very quickly. The mortality rate of startups in the early years is extremely high. You’re far more likely to die as a startup than you are of almost any disease in the world you could catch. It’s a very difficult thing to make work.
zh: 我认为这也是为什么贝佐斯的交易最终最终达成的原因，Jeff 实际上并不想买断我们的独立性。他并不想买入某种告诉我们怎么做的权利，我认为这刻画了当时我们交谈过的大部分其他 VC 的特征。但这也是一个事实，嘿，这是一张大支票。Jason 和我都没有多少名下的钱，我就更不用说了。我认为我们要有这种谦卑去想，你知道吗？这很可能就会结束。大多数事情很快就会结束。初创公司在早期的死亡率极高。作为一家初创公司死掉的可能性比你得上世界上几乎任何疾病的可能性都要高。要把这事做成是非常难的。

speaker: Unknown
en: So if you have some humility about that, you obviously should apply that to yourself and go, do you know what? This could not pan out. And right now we have something that’s hot that people are interested in, and they’re talking about big sums. And if we just go and we don’t do any of it and then it all blows up tomorrow, well, we’re going to have to find another job. And I would very much prefer not to have to find another job. So here’s the way out of that, but it clearly meant also giving up a lot of things. But again, I actually also think for both Jason and I, even when the stakes are as high as they can get for what we do, the decision usually comes quite quickly because there is this pre-processing that’s happening in your gut that tells you this is where it should go.
zh: 所以如果你对此有一点谦卑，你显然应该把它用在自己身上然后说，你知道吗？这可能会行不通。现在我们手头有热门的东西，人们对它感兴趣，他们在谈论大笔的金额。如果我们就这样什么都不做，然后明天全炸了，好吧，我们得去找另一份工作。我非常不想不得不去找另一份工作。所以这是一条出路，但这显然也意味着放弃很多东西。但再次，我也确实认为对 Jason 和我来说，即使赌注对于我们所做的事来说已经到了极限，决策通常来得相当快，因为你的直觉里有一种预处理，告诉你它该去哪里。

speaker: Unknown
en: I don’t think either of us really believe in long drawn out deliberation sequences. In fact, I always consider the smell. If we can’t make a decision quite quickly, it’s usually because there’s something right under the surface. It’s not lack of information. It’s some fear of some thing that if you just address that directly, the decision becomes obvious. So in this case, it was like, do you know what? Yeah, it’d be nice to have a couple million bucks in our bank account and therefore the confidence to go all the way and not be tempted by the VCs next month when they come with a bigger check or whatever, even if that means someone is on board with us. And the funny thing even with that decision was it could have gone back on it. In fact, I think 10 years ago, Jason and I seriously thought about, should we go back on it?
zh: 我们都不真正相信长期拖延的决策序列。事实上，我总是考虑这股“味道”。如果我们不能相当快地做出决定，通常是因为表面之下有什么东西。不是缺乏信息。是对某些事情的恐惧，如果你直接解决了那个问题，决定就变得显而易见了。所以在这种情况下，就像，你知道吗？是的，如果我们银行账户里有几百万美元就好了，因此有信心一路走下去，下个月 VC 带着更大的支票来的时候我们也不会受诱惑，即使这意味着有人和我们一起上船。关于那个决定有趣的是，我们本来可以反悔的。事实上，我认为 10 年前，Jason 和我认真想过，我们应该反悔吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: Should we buy Bezos back out of the business? Because we could have done it. And ultimately it just didn’t matter enough. The attraction to that idea was almost purely aesthetical. What if just the cap tables were just to the two of us again, would that not look nice or feel nice? It was not because we were like, “Oh my God, Jeff, keep your nose out of our business.” That was never the thing. We’ve had essentially the most idyllic, perfect, silent partner setup you could possibly imagine with Jeff along the way. But yeah, it was a one-way door. I think it qualifies.
zh: 我们应该把 Bezos 从业务中买断吗？因为我们可以那样做。但最终这根本没那么重要。那个想法的吸引力几乎纯粹是美学上的。如果股权结构表再次只属于我们两个人，那不是看起来或感觉起来很好吗？不是因为我们像，“天哪，Jeff，别管我们的闲事。”那从来都不是那回事。这期间我们和 Jeff 拥有本质上是田园般的、完美的、沉默的合伙人设置，你能想象到的最好那种。但是是的，那是一道单向门。我认为它符合条件。

speaker: Jason
en: I do think people would be absolutely shocked at how little we deliberate over pretty much anything. I mean, this really would surprise the hell out of people, I’m sure. It’s like when we make a call, we literally will have a five minute conversation about it. And sometimes there’ll be another one that’s seven minutes, but it’s kind of like, should we do this? Should we not do this? Yeah, yeah, no, yeah, whatever. We either get to both yeah or both no, and sometimes there’s a little bit of debate, but literally it rounds to zero for the most part. We just make decisions and we go for it because most everything can be reversed anyway. We’re rarely making massive decisions that are so filled with risk, so dripping with risk that we really have to be careful about it. And that’s by design. We try not to make those kind of decisions.
zh: 我确实认为人们会绝对震惊于我们对几乎任何事情的商议是多么少。我的意思是，这真的会让人们吓一跳，我敢肯定。就像当我们做一个决定时，我们真的只会花五分钟讨论它。有时会有另一个七分钟的讨论，但有点像，我们要做这个吗？我们不做这个吗？是的，是的，不，是的，无所谓。我们要么都得到“是”要么都得到“不”，有时会有一些争论，但大部分情况下字面上约等于零。我们只是做决定然后我们就去做了，因为几乎所有事情都是可逆的。我们很少做出充满风险、滴着风险的重大决定，以至于我们必须非常小心。这是设计使然。我们尽量不做那种决定。

speaker: Unknown
en: We try not to be a business that’s in that position. Sometimes you can get backed into a corner and force into that position. So far we haven’t been luckily for the most part, but even if we were, I think we’d make the call really quickly. If we decided at some point to sell the whole damn thing, honestly, it’d probably be a 15 minute conversation. We’re like, you know what? Fuck it. We’re done. Really, literally David, let’s say I said it first, David would be like, I’m feeling the same way. Or whatever. Or if he’s not or I’m not, we’d have another conversation, but it would not be months of deliberation about this and pros and cons lists and persuasion and it’d be like, yeah, let’s just move on or whatever. That’s kind of how it’s always been. I think that’s how it’ll always be. And I enjoy that very much.
zh: 我们尽量不做处于那种位置的业务。有时你会被逼到角落被迫进入那个位置。幸运的是到目前为止大部分时间我们没有，但即使我们是，我认为我们会非常快地做出决定。如果我们决定在某个时候把整个该死的东西卖了，老实说，这可能是一个 15 分钟的谈话。我们会像，你知道吗？去他妈的。我们要结束了。真的，字面意义上 David，假设我先说了，David 会像，我有同样的感觉。或者随便什么。或者如果他不是或者我不是，我们会有另一次谈话，但这不会有几个月的关于这个的商议，也没有利弊清单和说服，而会像，是的，我们就继续前进或者随便什么。这大致就是一直以来的样子。我认为这将永远如此。我非常享受这一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: It’s fun to just make calls and move forward fast and not get weighed down by things because ultimately at the end of the day, most things probably don’t matter. Basically, pretty much every decision you make in the business doesn’t really matter. It could have gone a hundred different ways and would’ve turned out the same way or differently. But the idea that this one decision you’re making was the only possible decision you can make at that time and that led to whatever else happened, there could have been a hundred other paths that led in the same way or not. Who knows? Nobody actually knows, but you’re better off just finding out by making a quick call and moving and seeing what happens, taking that next step and seeing where you are. That’s at least our perspective on it for the most part. So there’s nothing. There’s almost nothing that happens when we make a call.
zh: 做出决定并快速前进而不被事情拖累是很有趣的，因为归根结底，在一天结束的时候，大多数事情可能并不重要。基本上，你在业务中做的几乎每一个决定并不真正重要。它可能有一百种不同的走向方式，结果会是相同的或者不同的。但是你正在做出的这个决定是你在那个时刻唯一能做出的决定，并且它导致了随后发生的一切，这种想法本可能有一百条其他的路径导致同样的结果或不导致。谁知道呢？实际上没人知道，但你最好通过快速做一个决定、移动并看看会发生什么来发现，采取下一步并看看你在哪里。这至少是我们大部分时间对它的看法。所以什么都没有。当我们做决定时，几乎什么都没发生。

speaker: David
en: Now, I do think it’s important to stress that while the individual call is not that important, it’s because the net sum of all the calls really are, and that’s the moving average that we’re optimizing.
zh: 现在，我确实认为必须强调这一点很重要，虽然单个决定并不重要，这是因为所有决定的总和真的很重要，而这就是我们正在优化的移动平均值。

speaker: Jason
en: That’s right.
zh: 没错。

speaker: David
en: And what we have found in optimizing that moving average is that a great deal of humility must be applied to our intellectual ability to analyze a situation upfront that in almost all the cases, whatever the decision is, is usually one that asks reality for the check. What’s going to happen if we do this? And then we will adjust if that’s not quite right or that’s a little bit off. And that’s how we sort of go a little too high, a little under, and it averages out to a string of good decisions. I actually would take great pride that if you summarize 500 decisions we made, none of them had this sense that this was make or break, but the total sum of them totally did. If you make 500 decisions in a row and they all suck, you’re going to go out of business.
zh: 我们发现在优化那个移动平均值时，必须把大量的谦卑应用于我们在事前分析情况的智力能力，在几乎所有的情况下，无论决定是什么，通常都是一个向现实寻求支票的决定。如果我们做这个会发生什么？然后我们会调整，如果那不太对或者那有点偏差。这就是我们有点太高，有点偏低，然后平均出一串好决策的方式。我实际上会非常自豪，如果你总结我们做的 500 个决定，它们都没有那种成败在此一举的感觉，但它们的总和绝对有。如果你连续做了 500 个决定而且它们都很烂，你会破产。

speaker: Unknown
en: That is guaranteed. But if you don’t grip that hard on any individual decision, I actually think you are so much more likely to end up with a good string of decisions. And this is, Jason, remember you had this metaphor for loose hands for playing the drums. And I find that a lot of businesses and business owners and perhaps even more so executives have incredibly tight hands. They are really just gripping those Excel spreadsheets like their life depended on it. And in part, especially when they’re executive or they’re an owner who has owners, that is they’re an entrepreneur who has taken funding. So much of the decision making process is deliberation for show. I need the people who are watching me to feel like they’re going to have confidence in me because I have checked all the boxes and I’ve done all the spreadsheet and I’ve done all the analysis.
zh: 那是必然的。但如果你不对任何单个决定抓得那么紧，我认为你更有可能最终得到一串好的决定。这就是，Jason，记得你有过一个打鼓时手放松的比喻。我发现很多企业和企业主，甚至更是高管们，手都抓得非常紧。他们真的只是紧抓着那些 Excel 电子表格，就像他们的命取决于此一样。部分原因是，特别是当他们是高管或者他们是拥有老板的所有者，也就是他们是拿了融资的创业者。决策过程的大部分都是表演性的商议。我需要看着我的人感觉到他们会对我有信心，因为我勾选了所有的框，我做了所有的电子表格，我做了所有的分析。

speaker: Unknown
en: So if it goes wrong, can’t blame me. I did the math. I did the spreadsheet. So I mean, that’s just unforeseeable, right? And the great benefit for us is that we don’t have that second layer. There’s no one looking over us going like, did you do the math? No, we just get to hold the grips of the company really loosely. And I think it’s been that way since the beginning, but perhaps for me it’s gotten even more that way because you realize now that moving average that we’ve been playing on for 22 years, we have racked up so much that holy shit, we’ve probably, I don’t know if we could make 500 bad decisions in a row, but we could at least make 20. Twenty bad decisions just cold streak. We’re just batting out one thing after another. We’d still be here, still be allowed to do the business and run the things because we’ve created so much buffer over time.
zh: 所以如果出了错，不能怪我。我做了数学。我做了电子表格。所以我意思是，那只是不可预见的，对吧？对我们来说巨大的好处是我们没有那一层。没有人在我们上面看着说，你做数学了吗？不，我们只是可以非常宽松地握着公司的手柄。我认为从一开始就是这样，但对我来说可能现在更是这样，因为你意识到现在我们已经玩了 22 年的那个移动平均值，我们积累了这么多，该死，我们大概，我不知道我们是否能连续做 500 个错误的决定，但我们至少可以做 20 个。20 个错误的决定，只是冷 streak。我们只是在一个接一个地击球。我们还会在这里，仍然被允许做业务和管理事情，因为我们随时间建立了这么多缓冲。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that has given even more of loose hands, even more of an ability when Jason and I in rare instances don’t actually agree on something where I just go like, you know what? Yeah, I probably would’ve rolled it the other way, but who cares? Let’s just try it your way. And if it’s not working, I know as Jason does with me, reality’s going to tell the tale and we will just adjust. And therefore we can just have this incredible give and take and generosity of let’s just see where it goes. And then we don’t have to waste time in the deliberation room. And as Jason says, neither of us like that. I actually really like this sense of running right on the edge where I don’t know what the fuck I’m doing. Just slightly veering to the reckless side of being totally fucking ignorant about where it is and then just trusting I can hold my balance. Like you’re on a damn surfboard and you’re just going like, I don’t know why I’m still up here. I guess it’s something about micro movements one way or another. Man, it is bliss when it just sails through the ocean like that. And occasionally you wipe out it’s so fucking what? Get back onto the board.
zh: 这给了更多的手放松，更多的能力，当 Jason 和我在罕见的情况下实际上在某事上不一致时，我只是像，你知道吗？是的，我可能本来会以另一种方式做这件事，但谁在乎呢？让我们试试你的方式。如果它不工作，我知道就像 Jason 对我一样，现实会说明真相，我们就只是调整。因此我们可以只是有这种不可思议的宽容和慷慨，让我们看看它会去哪里。然后我们不需要在商议室浪费时间。就像 Jason 说的，我们都不喜欢那样。我实际上真的很喜欢这种就在边缘奔跑的感觉，我不知道他妈的我在做什么。稍微偏向鲁莽的一边，完全他妈的无知，不知道在哪里，然后只是相信我能保持平衡。就像你在该死的冲浪板上，你只是像，我不知道为什么我还在这里。我猜这是关于某种微动作之类的。伙计，当它就这样在海洋中航行时那是极乐。偶尔你摔倒了，那么他妈的又怎样？回到板上。

speaker: Jason
en: Can I actually add something really quick?
zh: 我能很快补充点什么吗？

speaker: Kimberly
en: Yeah, go ahead.
zh: 是的，请说。

speaker: Jason
en: This may be a bad example, but I think when you’re driving a car, you’re going somewhere, do you know how many decisions you’re making? You’re making a thousand decisions.
zh: 这可能是一个坏的例子，但我认为当你在开车时，你要去某个地方，你知道你在做多少决定吗？你在做一千个决定。

speaker: Kimberly
en: Without even thinking.
zh: 甚至都不用思考。

speaker: Jason
en: You’re just making decisions. And if you had to really think about every decision you make, you’d get nowhere. But we’re so comfortable with that idea. I feel like that’s how we run the business for the most part. There are a thousand decisions that we’re making all the time about a feature, an idea, how to respond to a customer, how to respond to... how to play with price, all the things. But we do it in a way where you’re driving, you are moving, you are not stopping every time you have to make a decision, you’re moving and making decisions. That’s how I think we do it. And I think if you start to think of your business as a car that’s moving and a deliberation is stopping, you’d be like, why are we stopping so frequently? Let’s just move and call, move and make calls, move and make calls, move and make calls.
zh: 你只是在做决定。如果你真的不得不思考你做的每一个决定，你哪里也去不了。但我们非常习惯这个想法。我觉得这就是我们大部分时间经营业务的方式。有一千个决定我们一直在做，关于一个功能、一个想法、如何回复客户、如何回复……如何玩弄价格，所有事情。但我们做的方式就像你在开车，你在移动，你不是每次要做决定时都停下来，你在移动并做决定。这就是我认为我们的做法。我认为如果你开始把你的业务想象成一辆正在移动的车，而商议就是停下来，你会像，为什么我们要这么频繁地停下来？让我们只是移动并决定，移动并做决定，移动并做决定，移动并做决定。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think that’s how you end up with a smooth curve essentially, which is kind of what David’s like... There’s errors that kind of maybe, ooh, that was close. I was tailgating this guy and I probably should have turned left when I turned right, but I’ll go around the block and get there anyway or wow, that was close or whatever. Or I scraped the tire when I was parked. Whatever it is, there’s things that go a little bit wrong. But for the most part, the curve is pretty smooth. You’re going in the right direction, you’re getting where you want to go, things are turning out all right. And it’s not that you don’t care about what you’re doing, you do, but you’re not stopping every time to make calls. I think that’s how I tend to at least think about it. I hate stopping the business is the way... I hate that. I don’t like that. We can’t do anything right now. We can’t do anything until we make this call. No, we’re going to keep doing things and we’re going to make calls as we go. That’s the way I like to think about it.
zh: 我认为这就是你最终本质上得到一条平滑曲线的方式，这有点像 David 像……有一些错误，可能有点像，噢，好险。我尾随那家伙跟得太近了，我可能应该向左转而不是向右转，但我会绕过街区并到达那里，或者哇，那很近或者随便什么。或者我停车时刮到了轮胎。不管它是什么，有些事情有点错。但大部分曲线是平滑的。你在正确的方向上，你要去你想去的地方，事情进展顺利。不是你不关心你在做什么，你关心，但你不是每次停下来做决定。这至少是我倾向于思考它的方式。我讨厌停下来做业务是那种方式……我讨厌那样。我不喜欢那样。我们现在不能做任何事。我们不能做任何事直到我们做出这个决定。不，我们要继续做事，我们会在过程中做决定。这就是我喜欢思考它的方式。

speaker: Kimberly
en: Okay. To go along with your analogy, has there ever been a period of time where you’ve been like, oh, we’re now not going in the right direction. We need to make a change because things are not going in the right direction.
zh: 好的。顺着你的比喻，有没有过一段时间你会像，噢，我们现在没有朝正确的方向前进。我们需要做出改变，因为事情没有朝正确的方向发展。

speaker: Jason
en: Well, yeah, there was at least one. I mean, back in 2021 when we had the no politics move. That was a moment where actually the business felt like it stopped.
zh: 嗯，是的，至少有一个。我是说，回到 2021 年当我们有那个“不谈政治”的举动时。那是一个业务实际上感觉停下来的时刻。

speaker: David
en: It was in reverse.
zh: 它在倒退。

speaker: Jason
en: Yeah. Well, yeah, it was going. Let’s carry the metaphor. Yeah. It was rolling down the hill. We’re up a hill. The clutch was in. We weren’t engaged and we were rolling back. We were about to hit someone behind us. That’s how it kind of felt. It’s not a good feeling and it kind of felt like it was chugging. It’s starting and stopping and starting and stopping around. There’s very staccato, which is a really shitty feeling. I think that’s how it feels. When the business is running its best, it feels like it’s moving forward. There’s wind in our hair and it’s a cool breeze. And this was a very stagnant moment and it didn’t feel right.
zh: 是的。嗯，是的，它在动。让我们继续用这个比喻。是的。它在往山下滚。我们在山上。离合器踩下去了。我们没有接合，我们在往后滚。我们要撞到我们身后的某人了。那就是那种感觉。这不是一个好的感觉，它感觉有点像喘气。启动和停止，启动和停止。非常断奏，这是一种非常糟糕的感觉。我认为这就是它的感觉。当业务运行得最好时，它感觉像在前进。风在吹着我们的头发，那是凉爽的微风。这是一个非常停滞的时刻，感觉不对。

speaker: Unknown
en: You know when you’re in traffic and you’re just stuck in traffic and it sucks and you hate it and it’s hot and there’s no wind and your air isn’t working, whatever it is. But the moment the traffic breaks and you get to go again, it’s just one of the best feelings, like open road again. That’s where we eventually got to, but we were in traffic for a long time and stuck with nowhere to go and it felt really terrible.
zh: 你知道当你堵在交通里，你只是困在交通里，这很糟，你讨厌它，很热，没有风，你的空调不工作，不管是什么。但是当交通疏通你又能走的那一刻，那只是最好的感觉之一，就像又是开阔的道路了。这就是我们最终到达的地方，但我们堵了很久的车，无处可去，感觉真的很糟糕。

speaker: David
en: But it also stands out because I don’t off the top of my head can remember any other moment that felt that stuck, that felt that gridlocked. I mean, we’ve certainly had moments where a product launch or feature launch didn’t go as well as you might have hoped or someone might have hoped. We try not to put too much hope into these things, but never to the point where it just felt like, oh man, I’m learning how to drive stick again and I’m constantly stalling the damn thing. That, now we’ve really tortured the metaphor to do. We can let it go now. We can let it drive off into the sunset. I think this is a good signal. It should not feel like that. That’s not normal. The normal thing is that the thing is moving and if you feel like you are stuck in this staccato moment and you got to change something, you’re going to burn out the clutch otherwise.
zh: 但它也很突出，因为我一下子想不起任何其他时刻感觉那么卡顿，感觉那么僵持。我的意思是，我们当然有过产品发布或功能发布没有达到你或某人希望的那样好的时刻。我们尽量不对这些事情寄予太大的希望，但从未达到感觉像，噢伙计，我又在学习开手动挡了，我不断熄该死的车。那个，现在我们真的把这个比喻折磨够了。我们现在可以让它走了。我们可以让它开进夕阳里。我认为这是一个好信号。它不应该感觉像那样。那是不正常的。正常的事情是它在移动，如果你感觉你卡在这个断奏的时刻，你必须改变点什么，否则你会烧坏离合器。

speaker: Kimberly
en: David, no more.
zh: David，别说了。

speaker: David
en: It is going to pop. You can’t stay in that moment. So it’s worth, if you are in that moment, to do something a little, I mean, reckless, maybe driving over the greens there to get on a different road. Okay, I’ll stop. And yeah, just don’t accept it. Don’t accept that. Do you know what? Most of the time in the 20 plus years we’ve been going, it has been smooth. Micro adjustments all the way as always. A little bit of, ooh, okay, maybe I should keep a bit more distance, but ..... don’t accept that. That’s not a way to live.
zh: 它会爆的。你不能停留在那个时刻。所以它是值得的，如果你在那个时刻，做点什么，我是说，鲁莽点的，也许从草坪上开过去以到达另一条路。好的，我会停下来的。是的，只是不要接受它。不要接受那个。你知道吗？在我们要走的 20 多年时间里，大部分时间它是平滑的。一直进行微调。有点像，噢，好的，也许我应该保持更远的距离，但……不要接受那个。那不是一种生活方式。

speaker: Jason
en: The other thing is we’ve made some decisions that haven’t panned out. I just don’t care. I’m not going to dwell on them. I’m not going to look back on them and do a postmortem. I’ve written about this where like, well, what went wrong? And you try to make up a reason. You don’t really know the reason. You find a reason and then you think that’s the reason and maybe it is and maybe it isn’t and who knows and who cares anyway? The next moment is going to be different than the previous moment. All these lessons aren’t really applicable necessarily. There’s probably some big picture directional things that are, but like, oh, next time we won’t do this. This happens all the time. David, we’ve talked about this. The outcome for these kind of meetings is we need to communicate better. It’s a communication problem. Had we just told the other team. Whatever. That was not the problem.
zh: 另一件事是我们做了一些没有成功的决定。我只是不在乎。我不会纠结它们。我不会回头看它们做事后分析。我写过关于这个，就像，嗯，哪里出了问题？你试图编造一个理由。你并不真正知道理由。你找到了一个理由，然后你认为那是那个理由，也许它是也许它不是，谁知道呢，反正谁在乎呢？下一个时刻将与前一个时刻不同

speaker: Unknown
en: That was the easy thing to grab at because they go, yeah, we didn’t talk enough. Obviously if we talked enough, it’d be better. It probably wouldn’t have been any different. Who knows what the difference is? But this idea of dwelling on things that didn’t go well or didn’t go quite as right as you wanted or didn’t work out exactly as you’d planned, who cares? What are you doing now? Where are you now? What are you working on now? Learn moving forward. Don’t look back. Learn moving forward. The next thing, make it better. Take your lessons from the things that work. And even those aren’t even totally clear because those are also a product of a moment, timing, market conditions, variables you don’t control, variables you don’t even know exist. Just do the best you can in the moment you’re in. Keep doing that as often as you can and it’ll play out the way it plays out.
zh: 那是最容易抓住的一点，因为他们会说，是的，我们交流得不够。显然如果我们交流得足够多，情况会更好。但可能也不会有什么不同。谁知道会有什么差别呢？但是这种纠结于那些进展不顺、或者没有完全如愿、或者没有完全按计划进行的事情的想法，谁在乎呢？你现在在做什么？你现在在什么位置？你现在在致力于什么？在前进中学习。别回头看。在前进中学习。下一件事，把它做得更好。从那些行之有效的事情中吸取经验。而且即使那些也不是完全清楚的，因为它们也是特定时刻、时机、市场条件、你无法控制的变量、你甚至不知道其存在的变量的产物。只需在你所处的时刻竭尽全力。尽可能经常地这样做，结果自然会按它该有的方式呈现。

speaker: Kimberly
en: Okay. That is a great place to wrap it up. REWORK is a production of 37signals. You can find show notes and transcripts on our website at 37signals.com/podcast. Full video episodes on YouTube. You can do that at 37signals.com/podcastquestion, or you can send us an email to rework@37signals.com.
zh: 好的。这是一个很好的结束点。REWORK 是 37signals 的制作。你可以在我们的网站 37signals.com/podcast 上找到节目笔记和文字记录。YouTube 上有完整的视频剧集。如果你有关于工作和经营企业的更好方式的问题想问 Jason 或 David，请给我们留言。你可以在 37signals.com/podcastquestion 上这样做，或者你可以发送电子邮件至 rework@37signals.com。
